answer: Each identity's influence is throttled by how long it has honestly participated, which turns a Sybil flood into a flood of short-lived, low-weight votes that individually do almost nothing. The reason this works is that the attacker must pay a real cost on every identity, so scale becomes a liability rather than an advantage. This means an attacker must choose: either run a few high-quality identities, or many worthless ones — and neither option beats honest participation. Consider a voyage as the anchor of the cost.
